blocks.h: On completing this chapter, the reader should be able to:

items.h: Explain the legal definition of an insurance broker, distinguish a broker from an agent in terms of legal relationship, client duty, and market function, and describe the significance of the broker’s fiduciary duty to the client.

Describe the Nigerian Council of Registered Insurance Brokers (NCRIB), its regulatory functions, the licensing requirements and minimum capital for insurance brokers, CPD obligations, and the changes to broker regulation introduced by NIIRA 2025.

Explain the client money rules applicable to Nigerian insurance brokers, including the requirement for segregated premium trust accounts, the deadlines for insurer remittance, and the consequences of client money breaches.

Describe the full insurance broking process (from initial needs analysis through market placement, quotation comparison, policy issuance, claims advocacy, and renewal management) explaining the broker’s obligations and value-add at each stage.

Distinguish between retail and wholesale broking, explain how the Lloyd’s market interface operates in the Nigerian context, and identify the classes of risk typically placed through wholesale channels.

Explain the role and commercial structure of reinsurance broking, describe the reinsurance broker’s relationship with cedant insurers and reinsurers, and identify the major international reinsurance broking groups active in Nigeria.
Describe the requirements and process for Lloyd’s accreditation of Nigerian brokers and explain how international insurance placements are structured for risks that exceed domestic market capacity.

Explain the fee structures used in Nigerian insurance broking, including brokerage commission, service fees, and contingent commissions, and describe the disclosure obligations imposed by NIIRA 2025 and NCRIB regulations.

Describe the specific characteristics of life insurance broking in Nigeria, including the advisory model for group life, the annuity placement process, and the design and management of employee benefit consulting engagements.
Apply best-practice principles to the design, governance, talent management, and growth strategy of an insurance broking business in the Nigerian market.

blocks.text: 18.1 Introduction: The Broker’s Unique Position in the Insurance Market

blocks.h: The insurance broker occupies a distinctive and legally precise position in the Nigerian insurance market. Unlike the tied agent, who represents the insurer and is legally the insurer’s agent, the broker represents the client. The broker’s commercial success depends on the quality of the advice and market access they provide to the organisations and individuals who retain them. Their legal exposure and professional reputation rest on how faithfully they serve the client’s interests, not the insurer’s.

This client-first orientation makes brokerage the most intellectually demanding form of insurance intermediation. A broker must understand the client’s risk profile deeply enough to design an appropriate insurance programme; understand the insurance market well enough to know which insurers offer the best terms for that specific risk; negotiate effectively with underwriters; compare and evaluate competing quotations against objective criteria; and manage the relationship between the client and the insurer through the full policy cycle, including claims. A broker who does all of this well is a genuine risk management partner for their client, not merely a commission-earning transaction facilitator.

The Nigerian broking market is a significant and growing segment of the insurance distribution landscape. Brokers account for a disproportionately large share of commercial and corporate insurance placements, group life, employee benefits, marine, aviation, engineering, and large property risks. In these lines, the complexity of the risk and the scale of the premium make broker-intermediated distribution the dominant model: direct purchase by large corporates without broker advice is uncommon, and insurer direct placement to large commercial clients without a broker is rarer still.

NIIRA 2025 has brought significant changes to broker regulation: tightened client money rules, updated minimum capital requirements, enhanced consumer protection obligations, and a clearer liability framework for professional negligence. This chapter addresses both the structural features of Nigerian insurance brokerage (its legal basis, regulatory framework, commercial mechanics, and practice disciplines) and the practical management requirements for building a compliant, profitable, and sustainable broking business.

blocks.text: 18.2 The Broker vs. the Agent: Legal and Fiduciary Distinction
18.2.1 Legal Definition of the Insurance Broker

blocks.h: An insurance broker is a person or company that, for remuneration, acts as an intermediary between a person seeking insurance and an insurer, in matters relating to the effecting of insurance. This definition, rooted in the Insurance Act and clarified by NIIRA 2025 and the NCRIB Act, has two critical elements: the broker acts between the client and the insurer (not as the insurer’s agent); and the broker does so for remuneration (commission, service fee, or both).

A company registered with NAICOM and a member of the Nigerian Council of Registered Insurance Brokers (NCRIB) that places insurance business with insurers on behalf of clients, for which it receives remuneration in the form of brokerage commission or service fees. The broker acts as the legal agent of the client (not the insurer) in all matters relating to the placement and administration of the insurance contract.

blocks.text: 18.2.3 The Broker’s Fiduciary Duty to the Client

blocks.h: The broker’s fiduciary duty is the legal and professional obligation to act in the client’s best interest at all times, placing the client’s interests above the broker’s own financial interests and above the interests of any insurer with which the broker deals. This duty is the defining feature of the brokerage relationship and the primary source of the broker’s professional liability.
The fiduciary duty gives rise to several specific obligations in practice:

items.h: Duty of care in advice: The broker must conduct a proper needs analysis, identify the client’s insurable risks, and recommend an insurance programme that is genuinely suitable for those risks. A broker who recommends under-insurance (to reduce the premium and protect the client relationship) or who fails to identify a material risk exposure is in breach of the duty of care.

Duty of disclosure: The broker must disclose all material information about the risk to the insurer on the client’s behalf. A failure to disclose can result in the policy being voidable by the insurer, leaving the client unprotected. The broker bears professional liability if the non-disclosure was within the broker’s knowledge or should have been identified by a competent broker.

Duty of confidentiality: Information provided by the client in the course of the broking relationship is confidential. It may not be disclosed to third parties (including the insurer beyond what is necessary for placement) without the client’s consent.

Duty to avoid conflicts of interest: The broker must not allow its own financial interests (the commission it will earn from a particular insurer) to influence the recommendation it makes to the client. Where a genuine conflict of interest exists, it must be disclosed to the client.

Duty to follow client instructions: The broker must execute the client’s instructions promptly and accurately. A broker who delays placing a cover that the client has instructed, and the client suffers an uninsured loss in the gap, is exposed to a professional negligence claim.

blocks.text: 18.3 NCRIB: Regulation, Licensing, and Professional Standards
18.3.1 The Nigerian Council of Registered Insurance Brokers (NCRIB)

blocks.h: The Nigerian Council of Registered Insurance Brokers (NCRIB) is the statutory professional body for insurance brokers in Nigeria, established by the Nigerian Council of Registered Insurance Brokers Decree 1991, which has been subsequently consolidated with the Insurance Act. NCRIB operates under the supervisory authority of NAICOM and performs a dual function: it is both the membership and professional standards body for the broking profession, and a co-regulatory body whose registration requirements must be satisfied before NAICOM will issue a broking licence.

NCRIB’s mandate includes: maintaining the register of all licensed insurance brokers in Nigeria; setting and enforcing the professional standards, code of ethics, and minimum competency requirements for broker membership; approving and monitoring continuing professional development (CPD) programmes for members; receiving and investigating complaints against member brokers; and representing the broking profession in regulatory and policy discussions with NAICOM and the Federal Government.

To operate as an insurance broker in Nigeria, a company must obtain: (a) a corporate brokerage licence from NAICOM; and (b) membership of NCRIB. Both must be maintained on an annual basis through the payment of fees and the satisfaction of ongoing compliance requirements.

blocks.title: NIIRA 2025: Minimum Capital and Licensing Requirements for Insurance Brokers

blocks.h: NIIRA 2025 has updated the minimum capital and licensing requirements for insurance brokers in Nigeria. Key requirements include:

items.h: Minimum paid-up share capital: NIIRA 2025 sets an updated minimum paid-up capital for insurance brokers. The increased threshold (above the previous ₦5 million requirement) is intended to ensure that brokers have the financial substance to meet their professional indemnity obligations and to operate sustainably.

Professional Indemnity Insurance (PII): All licensed brokers must hold an active PII policy for a minimum indemnity limit set by NAICOM. PII protects the broker’s clients against financial loss arising from the broker’s professional negligence or error. Evidence of PII cover is required at annual licence renewal.

Key officer qualifications: The Principal Officer and key technical staff of the broking firm must hold minimum CIIN qualifications (Diploma level or above) and have defined minimum years of relevant insurance experience.
Annual renewal: Broking licences must be renewed annually with NAICOM and NCRIB membership maintained. Non-renewal results in automatic suspension of broking authority.

Fit and proper assessment: Directors and principal officers of the broking company are subject to NAICOM’s fit and proper assessment, covering financial integrity, professional conduct history, and relevant experience.

blocks.h: NCRIB mandates Continuing Professional Development for all registered brokers and their key technical staff. CPD requirements are structured around an annual credit point system: members must accumulate a minimum number of CPD credit points per year through approved learning activities (NCRIB seminars and conferences, CIIN examinations and modules, approved third-party training programmes, and relevant academic qualifications).

CPD is not merely a regulatory formality: in a market undergoing the regulatory transformation represented by NIIRA 2025 (including Risk-Based Capital, IFRS 17, NDPA 2023 data protection, Insurtech licensing, and updated consumer protection frameworks) the technical competence of broking professionals must be continuously refreshed. NCRIB’s CPD programme is designed to ensure that the profession keeps pace with this transformation.

Failure to meet CPD requirements is a disciplinary matter within NCRIB’s jurisdiction. Members who fail to accumulate the required CPD points in a given year may have their membership status suspended pending remediation, which has direct implications for their firm’s NAICOM licence renewal.
NIIRA 2025 introduces several changes that directly affect the operational and compliance obligations of insurance brokers:

items.h: Consumer protection obligations: Brokers are explicitly included within NIIRA 2025’s consumer protection framework. Brokers must treat customers fairly, provide clear and accurate information about products and pricing, avoid mis-selling, and operate a complaints handling procedure that meets NAICOM’s prescribed standards.

Premium remittance deadlines: NIIRA 2025 tightens the premium remittance timeline for brokers. Premiums collected from clients must be remitted to the insurer within the prescribed period (30 days maximum under the standard provision, shorter periods specified in individual brokerage agreements). Late remittance constitutes a regulatory breach.

Disclosure of remuneration: Brokers must disclose their total remuneration (brokerage commission from the insurer, service fees from the client, and any contingent or volume-based commissions) before the insurance contract is concluded. The disclosure must be sufficiently detailed for the client to assess whether the broker’s remuneration creates a conflict of interest.

Claims advocacy obligation: NIIRA 2025 clarifies that the broker’s duties extend through the claims process: the broker must assist the client in preparing and presenting a valid claim, advocate on the client’s behalf in any claims dispute with the insurer, and not accept a claims settlement that is manifestly unfair to the client without the client’s informed consent.

blocks.h: When a client pays a premium to a broker, that money does not belong to the broker. It is held by the broker in trust for the insurer until it is remitted. This fundamental principle, that client money is not the broker’s money, is the foundation of the client money rules that govern all Nigerian insurance brokers.

A segregated bank account maintained by the insurance broker specifically for the receipt, holding, and remittance of client insurance premiums. The account must be kept entirely separate from the broker’s own trading and operating accounts. Money held in the Premium Trust Account belongs to the insurer (until the policy is in force) and to the client (in the event of a claim return or policy cancellation), not to the broker.

The requirement to maintain a separate Premium Trust Account is imposed by NAICOM’s broking regulations and reinforced by NIIRA 2025. The account must: be held with a bank approved by NAICOM; be designated as a trust account in the account title; not be used for any purpose other than the receipt and remittance of client insurance premiums; and be subject to regular reconciliation between the broker’s premium records and the account balance.

The speed at which brokers remit collected premiums to insurers has been a source of significant market conduct concern in Nigeria. Some brokers have historically used the float period (the time between collecting premiums from clients and remitting to insurers) as a source of short-term liquidity for their own operations. This practice is illegal: it constitutes a misappropriation of client money and a breach of the trust account obligation.

NIIRA 2025’s provision: premiums collected from clients must be remitted to the insurer within 30 days of collection or within the period specified in the brokerage agreement, whichever is shorter. For individual policies and retail business, many insurer-broker agreements specify shorter remittance periods of 7–15 days. For large corporate accounts paying annual premiums in a single payment, the negotiated remittance timeline may be structured to align with the client’s payment receipt.

The practical implication for brokers is that the Premium Trust Account must have sufficient liquidity to remit each premium as it falls due, without waiting for accumulated balances. A broker that has collected premiums but cannot remit because it has used the trust account balance for other purposes is in a critical regulatory and legal position.

blocks.title: Consequences of Client Money Rule Violations

blocks.h: Breaches of the client money rules (whether through failure to maintain a segregated account, late remittance to insurers, or misappropriation of trust account funds) carry severe consequences under NIIRA 2025 and general law:

items.h: NAICOM regulatory sanctions: Suspension or revocation of the broking licence; financial penalties; public naming of the broker firm and its directors on NAICOM’s sanctions register.
NCRIB disciplinary action: Suspension or expulsion from NCRIB membership; referral to relevant professional bodies; publication of the disciplinary outcome in NCRIB communications.

Civil liability: The broker is liable to the insurer for the full amount of any premiums not remitted by the contractual deadline, plus interest. The broker is liable to clients for any losses arising from coverage lapses caused by premium non-remittance.

Criminal liability: Misappropriation of trust account funds, using client premium money for the broker’s own purposes, constitutes criminal fraud under the Criminal Code Act and the Economic Crimes (Prohibition) Act, exposing the directors of the broker firm to personal criminal liability.

blocks.h: Practical risk management: brokers should reconcile the Premium Trust Account daily, maintain a premium tracking system that flags upcoming remittance deadlines, and never use the trust account for any operational expenditure whatsoever.

The insurance broking process is the end-to-end sequence of professional activities through which a broker transforms a client’s risk exposure into a properly structured, competitively placed, and actively managed insurance programme. It is not a single transaction; it is a continuous management cycle that runs from initial needs analysis through annual renewal and, when necessary, claims resolution.

The foundation of every broking engagement is a thorough understanding of the client’s risk profile. For a new commercial client, this involves a formal risk survey: the broker reviews the client’s operations, assets, liabilities, legal obligations, existing insurance programme, and uninsured exposures to produce a comprehensive picture of what needs to be insured, to what value, and under what conditions.

For a life insurance client (an employer seeking group life or a high-net-worth individual seeking personal insurance), the needs analysis addresses: the client’s existing life insurance coverage and any gaps relative to the mandatory statutory requirements or their own desired protection level; the financial position of the dependants who would be affected by an uninsured death or disability; the premium budget available; and any special risk factors (unusual occupations, health history, geographic exposure) that require specific underwriting attention.

The outcome of the needs analysis is a written Client Risk Report, a document that identifies all insurable exposures, recommends the insurance programme required to address them, and forms the basis for the broker’s market placement. For large commercial clients, this report is a formal deliverable; for smaller clients, it may be a less formal summary, but the discipline of documenting the needs analysis is essential for the broker’s professional liability protection.

Market placement is the process of presenting the client’s risk to insurers and obtaining terms. The broker prepares a Placing Submission (also called a market submission or submission document) that contains: a description of the risk being insured (the nature of the risk, its geographic location, its value, relevant loss history, and any risk management measures in place); the coverage terms required; the desired policy period; and any special conditions or warranties the client has agreed to.

The broker submits this document to selected insurers, those they assess as being most likely to offer competitive and appropriate terms for the specific risk. The selection of insurers for market approach is one of the most skill-intensive aspects of broking: an experienced broker knows which insurers have appetite for which risk classes, which underwriters will engage positively with unusual or complex risks, and which markets are likely to offer the most favourable pricing at any given point in the underwriting cycle.

For standard risks (straightforward group life, common personal lines), the market approach may be a simple online submission to multiple insurer portals. For complex risks (large group life schemes, executives’ keyman insurance, aviation hull, offshore energy), the placement may involve direct negotiation with lead underwriters at multiple insurers, potentially including international placements.

When quotations are received from the approached insurers, the broker’s task is to compare them on a like-for-like basis and produce a recommendation for the client. Premium is the most visible comparison point, but experienced brokers and sophisticated clients know that it is only one dimension of the comparison. A lower-premium quotation that excludes a material risk, or that comes from an insurer with a poor claims payment reputation, may represent worse value than a higher-premium quotation from a financially strong insurer with comprehensive coverage terms.

A professional quotation comparison document should cover: the proposed premium and any applicable taxes and levies; the coverage terms (what is covered and what is excluded); the insurer’s financial strength (NAICOM solvency ratio, credit rating if available); the insurer’s claims service reputation (as assessed by the broker from their own experience and client feedback); any special conditions, warranties, or conditions precedent to coverage; and the broker’s recommendation with its written justification.

Once the client accepts the broker’s recommendation, the broker confirms the placement to the chosen insurer and coordinates the policy issuance. The broker’s responsibilities at this stage include: verifying that the policy document reflects the agreed terms, conditions, and premium; checking that any special endorsements, additional coverages, or specific exclusions agreed in negotiation are correctly documented; delivering the policy document to the client in a timely manner; and providing the client with a plain-language policy summary that highlights the key terms, the sum assured, the premium payment schedule, and the claims reporting procedure.

For group life schemes, the policy issuance process includes the issuance of individual member certificates to each covered employee, the preparation of a scheme booklet explaining the benefits to members, and the setup of the scheme records in the broker’s management system.

Claims advocacy is one of the most valuable, and most differentiating, services a broker provides to its clients. When a client suffers a loss and makes a claim, the broker acts as the client’s advocate: it helps prepare the claim documentation; liaises with the insurer’s claims team on the client’s behalf; monitors the progress of the claim through the insurer’s assessment process; challenges any claim assessments or quantum offers that are unfair; and, where necessary, engages loss adjusters, legal counsel, or NAICOM’s dispute resolution mechanism to protect the client’s rights.

In the life insurance context, claims advocacy is particularly important for: contested death claims where the insurer disputes coverage (suicide exclusion, non-disclosure issues, or cause of death disputes); CI and TPD claims where the clinical evidence is complex and the policy definition creates interpretation challenges; and group life claims where the employer and the insurer disagree about a deceased employee’s membership status or benefit entitlement.

A broker that is absent or passive during the claims process has delivered only part of its professional value to the client. NIIRA 2025’s clarification of the broker’s claims advocacy obligation reinforces what the NCRIB Code of Ethics has always required: the broker’s duty to the client does not end at policy issuance.

The renewal of insurance policies is both a retention and a quality management opportunity. At renewal, the broker should: review the adequacy of the current programme (are all material risks still covered? Has the client’s risk profile changed?); review the insurer’s service performance over the past year (claims payment speed, communication quality, premium accounting accuracy); approach the market for competitive renewal terms if the existing insurer’s renewal terms are not competitive; and present a renewal recommendation to the client with the same rigour as the initial placement.

The most common failure in renewal management is treating it as an administrative exercise, automatically renewing on the existing insurer’s terms without reviewing either the coverage adequacy or the market competitiveness of the premium. This passive approach fails the client’s interest and, if the client subsequently discovers they were significantly over-paying or under-insured, exposes the broker to a negligence claim.

Retail broking is the direct client-facing broking model, in which the broker has a direct relationship with the ultimate insurance buyer, the individual, small business, or corporate client. The retail broker understands the client’s specific risk profile, advises on coverage, and places the insurance directly with one or more insurers. The retail broker receives brokerage commission from the insurer and/or service fees from the client.

Most Nigerian insurance brokers operate as retail brokers. Retail broking spans a wide range of client sophistication, from individuals purchasing personal accident or life covers to large multinational corporations managing complex employee benefit programmes. The common thread is the direct client relationship: the retail broker is accountable to the client for the quality of the insurance programme.

Wholesale broking is the placement of risks with insurers on behalf of other brokers (retail brokers) rather than on behalf of the ultimate insurance buyer. The wholesale broker does not have a direct client relationship; their client is the retail broker who has referred the risk to them because the wholesale broker has specialist market access or expertise that the retail broker lacks.

Wholesale broking in Nigeria is most relevant for: risks that exceed the capacity of the Nigerian domestic market and require international placement; specialist lines (aviation, marine, oil and gas, complex property) that require underwriting expertise that most retail brokers do not have in-house; and Lloyd’s placements, where the Lloyd’s market’s unique subscription structure requires a specially accredited broker to act as a wholesale intermediary.

The financial structure of wholesale broking involves a split of the brokerage commission: the insurer pays brokerage to the wholesale broker, who then pays a share (the ‘producing commission’) to the retail broker who referred the case. The client is informed of this arrangement as part of the broker’s remuneration disclosure obligation.

blocks.text: 18.7.1 The Role of the Reinsurance Broker

blocks.h: Reinsurance broking is the application of the broking function to the placement of reinsurance, placing risk on behalf of direct insurers (the cedants) with reinsurers, rather than placing risk on behalf of insurance buyers with insurers. The reinsurance broker’s client is the direct insurer; the markets are the global reinsurance community.

The reinsurance broker’s value-add is substantial and differs from direct insurance brokerage in important ways. Reinsurance brokers provide: access to the global reinsurance market, including markets (Lloyd’s syndicates, European continental reinsurers, Bermudian markets) that the average Nigerian direct insurer cannot access independently; actuarial and technical analysis of the cedant’s portfolio to structure the most efficient reinsurance programme; negotiation of treaty terms, including retention limits, commission rates, and reporting requirements; and post-placement services including premium accounting, claims notification, and recovery management.

The Nigerian reinsurance broking market is served by both domestic broking firms with reinsurance departments and the Nigerian affiliates of global reinsurance broking groups. Domestic cession obligations under NIIRA 2025 (which require direct insurers to offer a minimum proportion of their reinsurance to domestic markets before going international) create a structured market for domestic reinsurance brokers who facilitate the domestic cession process.

Reinsurance brokers in Nigeria are required to hold a NAICOM reinsurance broking licence (distinct from a direct insurance broking licence) and must be members of NCRIB’s reinsurance broking register. The capital and qualification requirements for reinsurance broking reflect the larger premium volumes and greater technical complexity of reinsurance business compared to direct insurance broking.

The major global reinsurance broking groups active in the Nigerian market include: Aon Reinsurance Solutions, Guy Carpenter (a Marsh McLennan company), Gallagher Re, Willis Re (now part of WTW: Willis Towers Watson), and Howden Re. These groups bring global capacity, proprietary catastrophe modelling tools, and relationships with every significant reinsurance market in the world. They serve the largest Nigerian direct insurers and the domestic reinsurers on major reinsurance programmes.

For life reinsurance specifically, the global brokers provide: YRT and co-insurance treaty design and placement; facultative life reinsurance for large individual risks; catastrophe life reinsurance programme design (pandemic and mortality catastrophe covers); and actuarial advisory services on treaty pricing and structure. Nigerian life insurers with significant individual life or annuity portfolios benefit from access to these services through an internationally-connected reinsurance broker.

blocks.text: 18.8 Lloyd’s Accredited Brokers and International Placements

blocks.h: Lloyd’s of London is a unique insurance and reinsurance marketplace, established in London in 1688 and regulated by the Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA). Lloyd’s is not an insurance company; it is a market in which individual syndicates (each backed by capital provided by Members, including corporate capital providers) underwrite risks. The Lloyd’s market has a global reputation for accepting unusual, complex, and large risks that conventional insurance markets decline.

For Nigerian insurers and large Nigerian corporations, Lloyd’s is relevant as a market of last resort for risks that cannot be fully placed domestically and as a specialist market for certain classes: aviation, marine hull, offshore energy, fine art, high-value properties, and Directors and Officers liability. Lloyd’s also provides life reinsurance capacity for very large individual life risks and for catastrophe life covers through its specialist syndicates.

Access to the Lloyd’s market is restricted to Lloyd’s accredited (or ‘registered’) brokers. A Lloyd’s registered broker has been approved by Lloyd’s to submit risks to underwriters in the Lloyd’s Room (now substantially conducted through the electronic platform Lloyd’s Exchange). Accreditation requires: the broker to meet minimum financial standards; to demonstrate compliance with Lloyd’s broker management requirements; to have at least one Approved Lloyd’s Broker Representative (a named individual with Lloyd’s signing authority); and to commit to ongoing compliance with Lloyd’s market requirements.

Very few Nigerian broking firms hold direct Lloyd’s accreditation. The more common pathway for Nigerian brokers to access Lloyd’s capacity is through a correspondance arrangement with an internationally accredited Lloyd’s broker, the Nigerian retail broker originates the risk, structures the placing submission, and passes it to their Lloyd’s-accredited correspondent who physically presents it to Lloyd’s underwriters. The split of brokerage commission reflects this two-tier arrangement.

When a risk exceeds domestic capacity (either because the sum at risk is too large for the Nigerian market or because the risk class is one for which specialist international underwriting capacity is required) the broker structures an international placement. The process involves:

items.h: Domestic market exhaustion: The broker first approaches all relevant domestic insurers to place the maximum portion domestically, satisfying NIIRA 2025’s domestic cession obligation before going international.

International submission: A placing submission is prepared in English (or the language of the target market) conforming to the format expectations of the relevant international market (Lloyd’s, London company market, Bermuda, Continental European markets).

Lead market selection: For subscription market placements (Lloyd’s, London market), a lead underwriter is approached first. The lead’s decision to offer terms sets the reference point for all follow underwriters, who typically follow the lead’s terms with their own line.
Slip completion: The placing slip or cover note records each underwriter’s committed line (percentage of the risk they accept). Once the slip is 100% subscribed, coverage is confirmed.
Policy documentation: A market reform contract (MRC) or equivalent policy document is issued, incorporating all terms agreed with the subscribed underwriters.

blocks.h: Brokerage commission is the primary remuneration source for most Nigerian insurance brokers. It is paid by the insurer as a percentage of the gross premium on each policy placed by the broker. The commission rate varies by class of business and is subject to NAICOM maximum commission regulations. The broker retains the commission after remitting the net premium (gross premium less brokerage commission) to the insurer.

Brokerage commission rates in Nigerian life insurance are broadly aligned with the agent commission rates described in Chapter 16: group life commission is capped at 9% of premium and single-premium annuity commission at 3% (NIIRA 2025 s.62(1)); individual life brokerage is typically 30–40% of first-year premium with 5–10% renewal, within NAICOM guidelines (not set in the Act). Agent commission may not exceed broker commission (s.62(3)).

In addition to or instead of commission, brokers may charge the client a direct service fee for professional services rendered. Service fees are more common in: complex programme design engagements where the advisory work is disproportionate to the commission earned on the premium; long-term retainer arrangements where the broker provides ongoing risk management advice beyond placement; and cases where the client prefers to pay a transparent fee and negotiate the net premium directly with the insurer.

Service fee arrangements must be documented in writing, agreed before the engagement begins, and disclosed to the insurer where the service fee is charged in addition to commission on the same risk. NIIRA 2025 requires that the total cost of the broker’s services, commission plus fees, be disclosed to the client before the insurance contract is concluded.

Contingent commissions (also known as profit commissions, volume bonuses, or override payments) are additional payments made by insurers to brokers based on the volume or profitability of business the broker places with that insurer over a defined period (typically a year). Contingent commissions create a structural conflict of interest: a broker who places more business with insurer A (to achieve a volume bonus) rather than insurer B (which may offer better terms for the specific risk) is prioritising their own financial interest over the client’s.

NIIRA 2025 and the NCRIB Code of Ethics require that contingent commissions be disclosed to clients. Where a contingent commission arrangement exists with an insurer, the broker must inform the client before placing any business with that insurer and must confirm that the recommendation is based on the client’s interest, not on the contingent commission arrangement.
The following is illustrative of a NIIRA 2025-compliant remuneration disclosure statement that a broker should provide to each client before concluding an insurance placement:
REMUNERATION DISCLOSURE: [Broker Firm Name]
For the Group Life Insurance programme placed on your behalf with [Insurer Name], our total remuneration is as follows:
• Brokerage Commission: 15% of annual premium, paid by the insurer. On your annual premium of ₦8,500,000, this amounts to ₦1,275,000.
• Service Fee: ₦350,000 (annual advisory retainer for scheme management, renewal management, and claims advocacy), payable by you.

• Contingent Commission: We have a volume bonus arrangement with [Insurer Name] under which we receive an additional 3% of annual premium if our total annual placement with them exceeds ₦50 billion. We confirm that this arrangement has not influenced our recommendation to place your business with this insurer; our recommendation is based on their competitive pricing and claims service record for group life schemes of this size.
Total broker remuneration on this placement: ₦1,625,000. This disclosure is made in accordance with NIIRA 2025 and the NCRIB Code of Ethics.

blocks.text: 18.10 Life Insurance Broking: The Advisory Model

blocks.h: Group life insurance is the dominant life insurance product placed through the broking channel in Nigeria. Almost all significant corporate group life schemes (those covering 100 or more employees, and particularly those involving high-sum-assured executive cover or multistate employer groups) are broker-placed. The broker’s advisory role in group life is distinct from the retail agent’s role in individual life: the group life broker advises the employer (the policyholder), not the individual employees (the assured lives).
The value the group life broker adds at each stage of the process:

items.h: Scheme design: The broker designs the benefit structure (death benefit levels [as a multiple of salary, a fixed sum, or a combination], accidental death benefit, disability cover, and any life and critical illness extensions) based on the employer’s HR strategy, budget, and statutory obligation.

Market placement: The broker submits the scheme to multiple life insurers simultaneously, with a standardised request for quotation that enables genuine like-for-like comparison. For schemes above the NIIRA 2025 group life sum assured threshold requiring actuarial sign-off, the broker ensures the submission includes all required actuarial data.

Insurer evaluation: The broker evaluates quotations not only on premium but on: the insurer’s financial strength; their claims turnaround performance on group life claims; the quality of their scheme administration platform; and the insurer’s experience in handling schemes of similar size and complexity.

Annual renewal management: At each annual renewal, the broker reviews the scheme’s claims experience, updates the membership census data, and re-approaches the market to ensure the employer is receiving competitive renewal terms.

blocks.h: The Retirement Life Annuity (RLA) market represents a growing broking opportunity as Nigeria’s Contributory Pension Scheme matures and retirement savings accumulate. An annuity broker, whether an independent IFA or a specialist retirement advisory firm, provides the retiree with access to multiple annuity quotations from all NAICOM-licensed life insurers offering RLAs, enabling a genuine market comparison.

The annuity advisory process requires a higher level of personalised advice than group life placement: the broker must assess each individual retiree’s health status, life expectancy expectations, income needs, and dependant obligations before recommending a specific annuity structure. An enhanced annuity (which pays a higher income to a retiree with a diagnosed health condition that reduces life expectancy) may be the optimal recommendation for a client who does not know this option exists.

The disclosure obligation in annuity broking is particularly stringent: the irreversibility of the annuity decision means that a recommendation error (advising a client to take a level annuity when an escalating annuity would better protect against inflation, or failing to recommend the joint life option to a married client) can result in a lifetime of inadequate retirement income. The broker’s file must document the full needs analysis and the basis for every recommendation made.

At the highest level of sophistication, the group life broker evolves into an employee benefits (EB) consultant: an adviser who helps employers design, manage, and communicate a comprehensive employee benefit programme that integrates life insurance, group health, pension, and other welfare benefits into a coherent total rewards strategy.

The EB consultant’s value proposition extends beyond insurance placement: they advise on total benefit cost benchmarking against the market; help the employer optimise the tax treatment of employee benefits; design the communication strategy that ensures employees understand and value their benefits; and monitor the performance of all benefit providers (insurers, PFAs, healthcare managers) against agreed service standards.

This higher-value advisory model generates fee income (not just commission) and creates a deeper, more durable client relationship than the transactional group life placement model. It also creates a compliance obligation: an EB consultant who gives advice on pension design or tax treatment that turns out to be incorrect faces professional liability exposure in multiple regulatory frameworks simultaneously.

blocks.text: 18.11 Building and Managing a Broking Business in Nigeria

blocks.h: A broking business in Nigeria can be built around several different commercial models, each with distinct revenue characteristics, capital requirements, and growth dynamics:

blocks.h: A well-run broking business requires three core technology investments:

items.h: Broking management system (BMS): A platform that manages the full policy lifecycle from client intake through placement, policy issuance, endorsement, claims tracking, and renewal. The BMS must integrate with the Premium Trust Account for real-time premium reconciliation. Key features: automated renewal diary; outstanding premium tracking; insurer accounting statements; client communication log.

CRM: A client relationship management system that records all client interactions, tracks the pipeline of prospective clients, manages renewal dates, and enables account-level profitability analysis. For a corporate broker, the CRM tracks multiple contacts within each client organisation (HR director, CFO, CEO) and the history of every interaction.

Compliance tracking system: A system that tracks: NCRIB membership renewal dates; staff CPD completion status; PII renewal dates; client remuneration disclosure documentation; and NAICOM regulatory filing deadlines. For a broking firm with regulatory obligations to multiple bodies (NAICOM, NCRIB, CIIN, NDPC for data protection), automated compliance tracking is a governance essential.

blocks.h: Professional indemnity insurance (PII) is mandatory for all licensed Nigerian insurance brokers under NIIRA 2025 and NCRIB regulations. PII protects the broker against claims from clients alleging that the broker’s professional negligence or error caused them a financial loss. Given the broker’s fiduciary duty to the client and the consequential losses that can arise from a placement error or negligent advice, PII is not a formality; it is the financial backstop of the entire business.

Key PII design considerations for a broking firm: the minimum indemnity limit must meet NAICOM’s prescribed minimum; the policy should cover claims arising from negligent acts, errors, and omissions by the firm and all its employees; the retroactive date should be as early as possible (preferably from the firm’s incorporation date) to cover claims arising from past advice; and the policy should cover regulatory defence costs, not just client compensation claims.

blocks.text: 18.11.4 Growth Strategy for a Nigerian Broking Business

blocks.title: Advisory: Building a Sustainable Growth Strategy for a Nigerian Insurance Broker

blocks.h: Growth in insurance broking is driven by three engines that must be managed simultaneously:

ENGINE 1: CLIENT ACQUISITION. New client acquisition in insurance broking follows one of three pathways: referrals from existing satisfied clients (the most cost-effective and highest-conversion pathway); targeted approach to organisations identified through market research as having inadequate coverage or overpriced programmes; and networking through industry associations, professional bodies, and the NCRIB community. A broker that relies on passive enquiry without an active prospecting strategy will find its growth rate constrained by the size of its existing referral network.

ENGINE 2: CLIENT RETENTION AND DEVELOPMENT. A broker that retains 90% of its clients year-on-year and grows the premium per client by expanding the scope of services provided (adding group health, EB consulting, or reinsurance advisory) can achieve significant revenue growth without adding a single new client. Retention is built on service quality: claims advocacy that goes above expectations, renewal management that consistently delivers competitive pricing, and proactive risk advice that prevents coverage gaps.

ENGINE 3: MARKET POSITIONING AND EXPERTISE. A broker that is known as the specialist for a specific industry sector (oil and gas, healthcare, financial institutions), a specific product line (group life and EB, annuities, high-net-worth personal lines), or a specific geography (federal government bodies, Lagos State corporations, a specific professional association) will generate organic referrals from within that sector and command premium fee rates for specialist advice.

Critical success factor: The managing director’s personal reputation and relationships are the most valuable asset of a Nigerian broking firm in its growth phase. A broker firm that is known, trusted, and respected by both its clients and the insurer community (as a firm that pays premiums on time, handles claims professionally, and gives sound advice) will consistently win business that a less-trusted firm cannot.
A company registered with NAICOM and a member of NCRIB that places insurance business with insurers on behalf of clients. The broker is the legal agent of the client, not the insurer.

The legal and professional obligation to act in another party’s best interest. Insurance brokers owe a strict fiduciary duty to their clients, including duties of care, disclosure, confidentiality, conflict avoidance, and following client instructions.

blocks.title: Nigerian Council of Registered Insurance Brokers (NCRIB)

blocks.h: The statutory professional body for insurance brokers in Nigeria, responsible for maintaining the broker register, setting professional standards, and co-regulating the broking profession alongside NAICOM.
A segregated bank account maintained by a broker specifically for client insurance premiums, held in trust for the insurer until remittance and for the client in the event of return premiums.
A document prepared by the broker describing a client’s risk in detail for presentation to insurers during the market placement process. Also called a market submission or submission document.

The broker’s role in assisting and representing the client throughout the insurance claims process, including documentation preparation, insurer liaison, dispute escalation, and settlement negotiation.
The direct client-facing broking model in which the broker has a relationship with the ultimate insurance buyer and places insurance directly with insurers.
The placement of risks with insurers on behalf of retail brokers rather than ultimate clients. The wholesale broker provides specialist market access or international placement capability.
The application of the broking function to the placement of reinsurance on behalf of direct insurers (cedants) with reinsurers.
The international insurance and reinsurance marketplace in London through which specialist syndicates underwrite complex, unusual, and large risks. Access is restricted to Lloyd’s accredited brokers.
A broker approved by Lloyd’s to submit risks to underwriters in the Lloyd’s market. Few Nigerian brokers hold direct accreditation; most access Lloyd’s through London correspondent brokers.
The remuneration paid by the insurer to the broker as a percentage of the gross premium on each policy placed. The primary revenue source for most Nigerian brokers.
A direct fee charged by the broker to the client for professional advisory services, in addition to or instead of brokerage commission.

Additional remuneration paid by an insurer to a broker based on the volume or profitability of business placed with that insurer. Must be disclosed to clients under NIIRA 2025 and the NCRIB Code of Ethics.

Insurance covering the broker against claims by clients for financial loss arising from the broker’s professional negligence, errors, or omissions. Mandatory for all licensed Nigerian insurance brokers.
The initial stage of the broking process in which the broker assesses the client’s risk profile to identify all insurable exposures and determine the appropriate insurance programme.
The highest-value form of group life broking, in which the broker advises employers on the full design, management, and communication of integrated employee benefit programmes.
The policy documentation format used in the Lloyd’s and London company markets, recording the agreed terms and the subscribed lines of each participating underwriter.
